title: Why fibre matters
content: Dietary fibre slows digestion, helps maintain stable blood sugar, and supports gut health. Most adults benefit from at least 25-30g of fibre daily, but typical diets fall well short of this. Lentils, whole grains, vegetables, and fruit with skin are strong fibre sources.

title: Sri Lankan fibre-rich staples
content: Dhal (lentil curry), kollu (horse gram), mukunuwenna, gotukola, and other leafy mallum dishes are excellent fibre sources common in Sri Lankan meals. A single serving of dhal curry can provide 6-9g of fibre.

title: Sugar and added sugar
content: Naturally occurring sugar in fruit is processed differently by the body than added sugar in sweets, desserts, and sweetened drinks. Health guidance generally recommends keeping added sugar under 10% of total daily calories. Evening sweets and sweetened tea are common sources of excess added sugar in Sri Lankan diets.

title: Reducing sugar without giving up dessert entirely
content: Swapping a sugary dessert for fresh fruit, reducing portion size rather than eliminating a treat entirely, and being mindful of sugar in tea are practical, sustainable ways to reduce added sugar intake without an all-or-nothing approach.

title: Sodium and blood pressure
content: Excess sodium intake is linked to elevated blood pressure over time. Most guidance suggests staying under 2,300mg of sodium per day. Home-cooked curries with moderate salt are generally more sodium-controlled than restaurant food or packaged snacks.

title: Managing sodium in Sri Lankan cooking
content: Coconut milk-based curries, dried fish (karawala), and pickled items (achcharu) tend to be higher in sodium. Balancing a high-sodium dish with lower-sodium sides, like plain rice and fresh vegetables, helps keep daily totals reasonable.

title: Protein needs and timing
content: Protein supports muscle maintenance and satiety. Spreading protein intake across meals, rather than concentrating it all at dinner, is generally more effective for muscle maintenance than the total daily amount alone.

title: Plant protein sources in Sri Lankan food
content: Dhal, chickpeas (kadala), soya, eggs, and fish are strong protein sources in a typical Sri Lankan diet. Combining rice with lentils provides a more complete amino acid profile than either eaten alone.

title: Carbohydrates and energy
content: Carbohydrates are the body's primary energy source. Whole grains and starchy vegetables digest more slowly than refined white rice or white bread, leading to steadier energy levels and less of a post-meal energy dip.

title: Rice portion awareness
content: Rice is a dietary staple and doesn't need to be avoided, but portion size matters more than avoidance. A measured cup of rice paired with vegetables and protein is more balanced than a very large uncounted portion.

title: Types of dietary fat
content: Unsaturated fats (found in fish, nuts, and some plant oils) are generally considered healthier than excessive saturated fat (found in coconut oil, ghee, and fatty meat) when consumed in large amounts regularly.

title: Coconut milk in moderation
content: Coconut milk is a defining ingredient in Sri Lankan curries and contains saturated fat. Using thinner coconut milk, or balancing a rich coconut curry with lighter sides, helps manage overall saturated fat intake across a day.

title: Daily hydration needs
content: General guidance suggests around 2-2.5 litres of fluid daily for most adults, though needs vary with activity level and climate. Water, plain tea, and king coconut water all count toward hydration; sweetened drinks add sugar alongside fluid.

title: Consistency over perfection
content: Nutrition research consistently shows that consistent, moderately good habits over time produce better outcomes than occasional perfect days followed by very poor ones. A pattern of balanced meals most days matters more than any single meal.

title: Calorie balance basics
content: Weight change is driven primarily by the balance between calories consumed and calories used by the body. Small, sustainable daily adjustments tend to be more maintainable long-term than large, aggressive calorie cuts.

title: Why crash diets often fail
content: Very low-calorie approaches often lead to muscle loss, low energy, and difficulty sustaining the diet long-term, frequently resulting in regained weight. Gradual, moderate calorie adjustments paired with adequate protein tend to be more sustainable.

title: Kottu roti nutrition context
content: Kottu roti is often high in calories and sodium due to oil, sauces, and processed meat/sausage additions. A lighter home-made vegetable kottu with less oil and more vegetables is a more balanced alternative to restaurant-style kottu.

title: String hoppers and hoppers
content: String hoppers (idiyappam) are a lower-calorie rice-flour option compared to fried hoppers (appa), which include coconut milk and are often cooked with oil. Both can fit a balanced diet in appropriate portions.

title: Balanced rice and curry plate
content: A well-balanced rice and curry meal includes a moderate portion of rice, a protein source (fish, dhal, or chicken curry), at least one vegetable curry or mallum, and a small amount of sambol, rather than being dominated by rice alone.

title: Meal timing and consistency
content: Eating meals at roughly consistent times helps regulate hunger cues and can reduce the likelihood of overeating later due to excessive hunger. Skipping meals entirely often leads to larger, less controlled intake afterward.

title: This is general guidance, not medical advice
content: Nutrition information provided here is general wellness guidance based on common nutrition principles. It is not a substitute for advice from a doctor or registered dietitian, particularly for anyone with an existing medical condition, pregnancy, or specific clinical dietary needs.
